projectBackground.name: Rail Depot Contract Administration — Claim Review
projectBackground.context: The contractor claims 21 days of delay and lost productivity after late design information.

manager.name: Helen Marsh
manager.note: A claim is a story proved by records. Show cause, effect, notice and quantum.

assignment.title: Assess the contractor's claim
assignment.brief: Quantify prolongation and productivity loss, apply contract principles and write the assessment.

documents.name: Delay Notice
documents.note: Contractor claims 21 days of delay; daily preliminaries £4,200.

documents.name: Productivity Records
documents.note: Unaffected 12 m² per hour; affected 9 m² per hour.

documents.name: Contract Clause
documents.note: Notice within 14 days of the event.

tasks.title: Prolongation Cost
tasks.prompt: 21 days of delay with daily preliminaries of £4,200. What is the claimed cost (£)?
tasks.mistake: Claiming profit on time-related cost may not be allowed.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

tasks.title: Productivity Loss (Measured Mile)
tasks.prompt: Unaffected output 12 m²/h; affected 9 m²/h. What is the loss (%)?
tasks.reasoning: The measured mile compares affected with unaffected work.
tasks.mistake: Comparing with a planned rate only is weaker evidence.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

tasks.title: Concurrent Delay
tasks.prompt: Employer and contractor delays occur at the same time on the critical path. Common approach?
options: Time extension may be granted but costs usually not for the concurrent period
tasks.reasoning: Concurrent delay often gives time, not money.
tasks.mistake: Assuming full cost claims inflates quantum.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

tasks.title: Notice
tasks.prompt: The clause requires notice within 14 days of the event. Notice was given on day 30. What follows?
options: The claim may be time-barred depending on the clause and law
tasks.reasoning: Notice provisions can be conditions precedent.
tasks.mistake: Ignoring notice terms ruins good claims.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

tasks.title: Claim Evidence
tasks.prompt: Select useful evidence for a delay claim.
options: Records of instructions and late information
Memory of site staff months later
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

tasks.title: Assessment Summary
tasks.modelAnswer: The contractor claims 21 days at £4,200 per day (£88,200). The critical path analysis supports 14 days caused by late design information, so I assess time at 14 days. Notice was given on day 18 against a 14-day requirement; the clause is not clearly a condition precedent, so entitlement is recommended subject to legal advice. Productivity loss of 25% requires better records before it can be accepted.
tasks.reasoning: A good assessment separates entitlement, time and cost.
tasks.mistake: Accepting totals without analysis is risky.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

caseStudy.title: Case Study: The Claim With No Records
caseStudy.background: A contractor lost most of a £2M claim because daily records and instructions were not kept. The tribunal accepted only what documents proved.
caseStudy.solution: Sterling requires contemporaneous records and monthly programme updates.
